text: Say to yourself at the start of the day: I shall meet with the meddlesome, the ungrateful, the insolent, the deceitful, the envious, the unsocial. All these things befall them because of their ignorance of what is good and what is evil. But I, who have observed the nature of the good — that it is beautiful — and of the bad — that it is ugly — and the nature of the wrongdoer himself — that he is akin to me, not by the same blood or seed, but as a participant in mind and in a portion of the divine — I can neither be harmed by any of them, for no one can cover me with what is ugly; nor can I be angry with my kinsman, nor hate him. For we are born for cooperation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of the upper and lower teeth. To act against one another is therefore contrary to nature; and to be vexed and to turn away is to act against one another.
review_notes: English translation of Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book II, section 1. The translation prioritizes semantic precision and the preservation of the logical sequence of the original: anticipation of difficult encounters, explanation rooted in ignorance of good/evil, recognition of shared rational nature, conclusion about invulnerability to harm and the duty of cooperation, and the organic metaphor. Key choices: 'meddlesome' (περιέργῳ), 'insolent' (ὑβριστῇ), 'unsocial' (ἀκοινωνήτῳ), 'beautiful' (καλόν) and 'ugly' (αἰσχρόν) for the aesthetic-moral vocabulary central to Stoic ethics, 'participant in mind' (νοῦ...μέτοχος), 'cover me with what is ugly' (αἰσχρῷ...περιβαλεῖ). The translation of 'καλόν/αἰσχρόν' as 'beautiful/ugly' rather than 'honourable/shameful' preserves the sensory-aesthetic dimension of Stoic moral vocabulary. Requires human review, especially for the Stoic technical vocabulary.
